## Proof

1.1 The initial admission checks terminate: the format's subnormal index
range, exponent range and significand ranges are finite, and each equality
comparison of exact dyadics is decided by clearing powers of two and comparing
integers. Their enumeration is exactly the selected representable set, so a
passing endpoint test establishes membership, including for zero and
subnormals. Invalid initial data stop before an evaluator call. For admitted
data, every endpoint of the initial box belongs to that format. Inductively,
a split enqueues children only after the exact midpoint passes the same
membership test; all other endpoints are inherited from the parent.
The DAG, output, constants, format and $N$ are unchanged. Hence every queued
box satisfies the elementary evaluator's input conditions. Each such call
terminates through its finite DAG, finite series, finite bisection and finite
bin/cell/quadrant lists, or returns a specified failure. The membership guard
also terminates and can stop immediately with `inconclusive`. There are at
most $B$ admitted splits and therefore at most $2B+1$ processed boxes.
Thus the entire procedure terminates, including every guard-stop branch.
[given, L1, algebra, induction]

1.2 Before a box is processed, the completed leaf boxes together with the
queued boxes cover $X$. Removing a current box preserves this cover when that
box is counted as the current unresolved parent. Completing it transfers it
to the completed leaves; an admitted split replaces it by two closed children
whose union is the parent by [L1]. A failed midpoint test retains the parent
as unresolved and therefore discards no part of the cover. This proves the
coverage invariant by induction. By step 1.1, each completed leaf was evaluated
on admissible input, so its finite enclosure contains its exact range by [L2]
or [L3]. If the queue empties without an early return, all covering leaves are
completed; their enclosure hull therefore contains the exact range on all of
$X$. On an early return, the completed-leaf hull is not asserted to cover the
unresolved parent or remaining queue. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, induction]

1.3 A `certified` return occurs only after the queue is empty without an
admission, evaluator, split-guard or budget stop, and after the completed-leaf
hull passes the final global width test. Step 1.2 then proves enclosure of the
whole range, and the exact width comparison proves the requested tolerance.
A failed midpoint membership instead returns `inconclusive` with the
completed-leaf hull, unresolved parent, remaining queue and actual guard
status; that partial hull is not a full-domain certificate. The other
non-finite, exhausted-budget, unsplittable-coordinate and failed global-width
branches likewise make no tolerance-success claim. Thus the finite guard
preserves the stated certified-range, coverage and failure conclusions.
[given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Proof

1.1 Let $Z=X+iY$ be a rectangle. By [L1], its exact exponential has real and
imaginary parts $\exp(X)\cos(Y)$ and $\exp(X)\sin(Y)$. The real enclosures in
[L2] contain these three ranges, and rectangle multiplication and addition
preserve their exact component images by [L3]. Therefore the resulting
rectangle contains $\exp(Z)$. [given, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

1.2 For a principal-log branch, subdivide $Z$ into rectangles of fixed signs
of the real and imaginary coordinates, with separate pieces on the coordinate
axes. In a nonzero quadrant, $|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ is enclosed by [L2]–[L3],
hence $\ln|z|$ is enclosed by [L2]. The quotient is enclosed by [L3] and
arctangent by [L2]. In quadrant I use $\arctan(y/x)$; in quadrant IV use
$-\arctan((-y)/x)$; in quadrant II use $\pi-\arctan(y/(-x))$; and in
quadrant III use $-\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x))$. From [L4] and
$\sin^2(A(t))+\cos^2(A(t))=1$, positivity of $\cos(A(t))$ gives
$\cos(A(t))=1/\sqrt{1+t^2}$ and
$\sin(A(t))=t/\sqrt{1+t^2}$ for $t>0$. Substituting $t=y/x$ in quadrant I
gives $(\cos\operatorname{Arg}z,\sin\operatorname{Arg}z)=(x/|z|,y/|z|)$.
In quadrant IV, evenness/oddness from [L1] gives the same coordinate
identity with $y<0$. The addition identities shift the angle in quadrant II
by $\pi-A(t)$, reversing only the cosine sign, and in quadrant III by
$-\pi+A(t)$, reversing both signs; substitution of the positive coordinate
ratios again gives $(x/|z|,y/|z|)$. The range of $A$ in [L4] places these angles in the respective
subintervals of $(-\pi,\pi)$, so they are the principal arguments. On the
admissible closure of quadrant I the argument lies in $[0,\pi/2]$; on
quadrants II, III and IV it lies respectively in $[\pi/2,\pi]$,
$[-\pi,-\pi/2]$ and $[-\pi/2,0]$. Since $p_-\le\pi\le p_+$ and
$p_->0$, these sets are contained respectively in the algorithm's fixed
sectors $S_{\rm I},S_{\rm II},S_{\rm III},S_{\rm IV}$. A finite raw
ratio-based argument interval contains each exact argument by [L2]–[L3],
so intersecting it with its sector retains every exact argument. Each
nonempty quadrant piece has an actual point and hence an argument in that
intersection; an empty intersection cannot be used for a success claim and
is explicitly rejected. When the denominator reaches zero, the sector alone
is a sound enclosure. The common final outward conversion $H$ preserves
these containments; an overflow gives no finite claim.

On the positive real axis the exact argument is zero, and on the positive
and negative imaginary axes it is respectively $\pi/2$ and $-\pi/2$.
Thus $H([0,0])$, $H(P_N/2)$ and $H(-P_N/2)$ enclose the axis values.
The initial domain test excludes the origin and negative real axis. The
strict-sign pieces, their closures and these axis pieces therefore cover
every admissible point. The radial enclosure established above and the
converted argument enclosure jointly contain its principal logarithm;
taking the coordinatewise hull over every finite piece contains the full
image. Any failed piece prevents a finite hull return.
[given, L1, L2, L3, L4, construct, algebra]

1.3 Fix the DAG, designated output, constant enclosures, format and $N$ in
the Statement, so both calls use the same $P_N$, sectors and conversion $H$.
Every nonempty strict-sign piece of a smaller input rectangle, after closure,
is contained in the corresponding piece of the larger rectangle. Every axis
piece likewise has a corresponding containing axis piece, with the same
argument interval. The radial expression $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ preserves
inclusion on these nested pieces by [L2]–[L3].

For a quadrant whose denominator excludes zero in both calls, outward
quotients and the fixed real arctangent evaluator give nested finite raw
argument intervals $A\subseteq A'$ by [L2]–[L3]. Exact translations by the
same $P_N$ and sign changes in the quadrant formulas preserve this inclusion.
Intersection with the same sector gives
$A\cap S_q\subseteq A'\cap S_q$. The greatest-lower and least-upper
rounding definitions make $H$ inclusion-preserving, hence the converted
argument intervals are nested as well. If enlargement changes a ratio branch
to a zero-denominator coarse branch, the smaller preconversion interval is
$A\cap S_q\subseteq S_q$, and therefore
$H(A\cap S_q)\subseteq H(S_q)$. If both branches are coarse they use the
same $H(S_q)$. The reverse change under enlargement is impossible: a
containing denominator interval cannot exclude zero when the smaller one
contains it. These cases exhaust quadrant branch transitions. Axis pieces
remain present under enlargement and use the identical converted axis
intervals, so their corresponding rectangles are nested too.

Taking coordinatewise hulls preserves the inclusions for all corresponding
pieces, including any additional pieces in the larger call. Complex
exponential preserves inclusion through its fixed real component evaluations
and rectangle operations in step 1.1. Together with [L2]–[L3], these primitive
results give soundness and inclusion for the same finite typed DAG by
induction in its prescribed topological order; fixed input-independent
constants start the induction, and every designated output inherits it.
A rectangle meeting zero or the negative real branch cut at a Log node
returns `domain-error`; a failed piece, empty argument intersection or failed
conversion returns its specified non-finite status. Such a branch gives no
finite enclosure or nesting claim.
[step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra, induction] ∎

## Verification

1.1 Apply [L1] at $1/5$ and $1/239$ with $N=12$. The arctangent interval
widths are at most twice the displayed tails; multiplying by $16$ and $4$
gives the two rational terms in the bound. By [L4], the integral gives
$13/20\le\arctan1\le9/10<1$: its integrand is at least $4/5$ on
$[0,1/2]$ and at least $1/2$ on $[1/2,1]$, while it is at most $1$ on the
first half and at most $4/5$ on the second. Thus
$13/5\le\pi\le18/5<4$. Before rounding, the Machin interval has width less
than $2\cdot10^{-19}+10^{-30}$ by the tail estimates below, so its exact
endpoints lie in $[5/2,37/10]$ using $13/5\le\pi\le18/5$. The directed
conversions stay in that interval and therefore each add at
most $2^{-126}$ to the width. For the first tail,
$32(1/5)^{27}/(27(1-1/25))=800/(648\cdot5^{27})<2\cdot10^{-19}$, using
$4000\cdot10^{18}<648\cdot5^{27}$. The second tail is less than
$239^{-27}<16^{-27}=2^{-108}<10^{-30}$. Therefore exact rational comparison gives
$W:=\operatorname{width}(P)<10^{-18}$ and $\pi\in P$.
[given, L1, L2, L4, algebra]

1.2 Each $x\in X$ has form $x=2p$ with $p\in P$, so
$|x-2\pi|=2|p-\pi|\le2W<2\cdot10^{-18}<\inf(P)/4\le\pi/4$;
$\inf(P)\ge5/2$ by step 1.1. Thus $X$ lies inside the canonical $k=4$ cell. If
$P=[p_-,p_+]$, the actual cell formula
$C_k=kP/2+[-1/4,1/4]P$ gives
$\sup C_3=7p_+/4$ and
$\inf C_5=5p_-/2-p_+/4=9p_-/4-W/4$.
Since $p_->2$ and $W<10^{-18}$, both $p_->7W$ and $p_->9W$ hold.
Consequently
$2p_- -\sup C_3=(p_--7W)/4>0$ and
$\inf C_5-2p_+=(p_--9W)/4>0$.
Thus $X=2P$ meets neither neighboring enclosure. All farther cells are
separated as well by monotonicity of their endpoints in the integer cell
index, while $C_4$ contains $X$. Hence the only included candidate is $k=4$. The interval residual computed by the evaluator is
$R=X-4(P/2)=[-2W,2W]$, which contains each exact reduced argument and lies
inside the certified Taylor range. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

2.1 Put $r_0=2W<2\cdot10^{-18}$. Bound each odd Taylor term on
$R=[-r_0,r_0]$ by the symmetric exact rational interval
$[-r_0^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!,r_0^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!]$, sum these intervals exactly,
and add the geometric tail before outward conversion. The polynomial interval
has total width at most
$2\sum_{k=0}^{12}r_0^{2k+1}/(2k+1)!\le2r_0/(1-r_0^2)<6\cdot10^{-18}$,
since $r_0^2<1/3$ gives $(1-r_0^2)^{-1}<3/2$.
Since $r_0<1/2$, the displayed tail formula gives
$T_s<2r_0^{27}/27!<2r_0^2<10^{-18}$, so the symmetric tail width is below
$2\cdot10^{-18}$. Only four directed endpoint conversions occur in this
exact-rational path (two for $P$ and two for the sine enclosure); their total
width increase is at most $4\cdot2^{-126}$, below the conservative allowance
$200\cdot2^{-126}$. The total width is therefore below $1$. With $B=0$, the
budgeted evaluator checks this finite
enclosure and returns `certified`; [L3] confirms the exact range and width
claim. No system sine routine is used. [step 1.2, given, L2, L3, algebra] ∎
